news.abstract: Excelsior, once prominent newspaper of Mexico, is bought by group of unidentified American and Canadian investors for $150 million; 25 years ago rulers of Institutional Revolutionary Party secretly bought newspaper's loyalty and over time drained it of independence; when Pres Vicente Fox's election ended Institutional Revolutionary Party's control, under-the-table subsidies and payoffs ended, and newspaper quickly fell into near bankruptcy (M)
news.title: A Mexican Daily's Downfall

news.abstract: Turkey says US may not deploy substantial numbers of ground troops on its territory in event of war with Iraq; new government, led by party with Islamist roots, says US may station warplanes and use Turkish air space to carry out air strikes, but only if UN Security Council adopts new resolution authorizing use of force; Min Yasar Yakis cites Turkish public opinion in presenting position to Deputy Sec Paul D Wolfowitz; photo; map; Turks do not preclude stationing of Special Operations force and small ground units (M)
news.title: TURKEY SAYING NO TO ACCEPTING G.I.'S IN LARGE NUMBERS

news.abstract: HAITI: Protests Are Stopped; MEXICO: Toll Rises In Bus Crash;.
news.title: World Briefing: The Americas

news.abstract: Trial begins for leading Iranian reformist politician and pollster Akbar Abdi along with two other pollsters; numerous charges against them include manipulation of public opinion polls (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Middle East: Iran: Pollsters Go On Trial

news.abstract: President Bush has invited Recep Tayyip Erdogan to Washington in an effort to win broader support from Ankara for a possible military campaign in Iraq.
news.title: Bush to Press Turkish Leader for Military Support on Iraq

news.abstract: British government offers compromise proposal that would end annual divisive debate by banning fox hunting in some areas and licensing it in places where it could be justified as pest control; stag and hare hunting would be banned altogether (S)
news.title: British Plan Would Spare Some Fox Hunting

news.abstract: Investigators close aÿ
news.title: Dutch Shut IKEA Stores After Bombs Are Found

news.abstract: Iraqi liaison with United Nations arms inspectors, Maj Gen Hussam Muhammad Amin, launches furious broadside against inspectors for their no-notice search of one of Pres Saddam Hussein's innumerable palaces and ascribes it to pressures from United States, Britain and Israel; holds news conference to again deny that Iraq has any banned nuclear, chemical or biological arms; day's events suggest conflicting pressures building in Baghdad, 72 hours before Iraq promises to deliver declaration on any secret weapons programs; Saddam Hussein will seek to meet UN's demands in ways that avoid war while saving his prestige, if not his weapons programs; Amin suggests that inspectors' palace visit was intended to humiliate Hussein; Iraq Foreign Ministry questions why inspectors did not wear protective suits for palace visit if they suspected there might be biological, chemical or nuclear weapons there (M)
news.title: Iraq Denounces Visit to Palace By U.N. Team

news.abstract: Venezuelan businessmen and workers opposed to Pres Hugo Chavez's government extend paralyzing general strike into fourth day, possibly damaging informal accord made earlier in day between government and its foes in talks mediated by Organization of American States; strike threatens to cripple economy and disrupt oil supplies to United States; government had agreed in talks not to block nonbinding Feb 2 referendum on whether Chavez should stay in office and signaled that it would be open to talks on holding early presidential elections (M)
news.title: Chávez's Foes Plan to Extend General Strike In Venezuela

news.abstract: Sec Colin L Powell says United States will increase military aid to Colombia to over $500 million a year, holding its war on leftist guerrillas and rightist paramilitary groups, and on their drug trafficking, is part of Bush administration's drive against terrorism; aid will be used for drug eradication, support for military and police forces and renewed support for Colombian narcotics-interception flights that rely on intelligence from American spy planes; Powell meets with Pres Alvaro Uribe Velez, Bogota; holds terrorism and drugs are linked in Colombia as threats to democracy; photo (M)
news.title: Powell Says U.S. Will Increase Military Aid for Colombia

news.abstract: Indonesian police arrest Ali Ghufron, better known as Mukhlas, who is suspected of being senior commander in regional terrorist network Jemaah Islamiyah and key participant in Bali attack; diplomats and security officials hail arrest, in central Java, as big step in learning more about network and its links to Al Qaeda; he is brother of Amrozi, one of first people arrested in connection with Oct nightclub bombing; is also wanted in Singapore in Dec 2001 plot to blow up American Embassy there; arrest marks toughening in Indonesian government's attitude and policy toward terrorism; fact that he had not fled Indonesia raises questions about whereabouts of other Qaeda members and whether their list of potential hiding places is dwindling; United States and Australia are now focusing search for terrorists in area that includes southern Philippines and remote reaches of Borneo, island divided between Indonesia and Malaysia (M)
news.title: Indonesia Holds Suspect In Bombings At Bali Clubs

news.abstract: PARIS—  As the world's purveyors of luxury goods huddle over designer-bag strategies in hopes that world turmoil will be averted and customers won't stop shopping, fashion in the Middle East is alive and kicking.
news.title: Caftans and hothouse glamour:Mideast couture heats up

news.abstract: Pres Alejandro Toledo of Peru, who was forced in October to acknowledge 14-year-old Zarai Toledo as his daughter after 13 years of court battles and increasingly public denials, now declares that he and Zarai are opening new chapter in their lives and that he has won 'an intelligent and beautiful daughter'; photos (M)
news.title: Piura Journal; At 14, the Girl's Indomitable (Just Ask Her Father)

news.abstract: Akhmed Zakayev, senior Chechen representative at center of angry extradition dispute between Russian and Danish officials, leaves Denmark for Britain, raising prospect of similar dispute with British authorities (S)
news.title: Chechen Fugitive on His Way to Britain

news.abstract: COTTBUS, Germany:—  No one is entirely sure why so many women in this quaint, cobblestoned city south of Berlin stopped having babies 10 years ago. But it does not take a degree in sociology to see the effects of the rock-bottom birthrate: Thousands of schoolteachers have been laid off for lack of students. Workers have begun to dismantle, piece by piece, dozens of vacant apartments, part of a plan to demolish 5,000 units over the next decade. And the municipal water system is in need of a costly overhaul because water use is decreasing and stagnant water in pipes is a health hazard.
news.title: IHT Insight: Low birthrates pose challenge for Europe

news.abstract: Brushing aside objections, the Hong Kong today ended a public comment period on plans for tough internal security laws and said it would proceed directly with legislation.
news.title: Brushing Aside Objections, Hong Kong Proceeds on Security Law

news.abstract: North Korea has started to reopen sealed plutonium reprocessing plant at Yongbyon nuclear complex, most provocative and technically important step it has taken in recent days to revive its nuclear arms program; International Atomic Energy Agency says North Koreans have disabled surveillance cameras and broken through seals at pool holding 8,000 spent fuel rods; Bush administration stresses it will continue to deal with situation diplomatically; Defense Sec Donald H Rumsfeld warns United States is capable of confronting North Korea militarily, news conference; bipartisan pressure grows from Congress for Bush to rethink policy of not negotiating until North Korea drops nuclear program; photos; map (M)
news.title: North Korea Begins to Reopen Plant for Processing Plutonium

news.abstract: Council on Foreign Relations, December 2002 - Les Gelb, the president of the Council on Foreign Relations, says that he is surprised by the degree of opposition in the United States to an invasion of Iraq. On a recent speaking tour, Gelb says 80 to 90 percent of audience members were against an invasion, which he says is likely by March unless Saddam Hussein is first overthrown through a coup. To get the public on its side, Gelb said it was imperative for the Bush administration to provide "a smoking gun" - conclusive evidence - that Saddam has weapons of mass destruction. On other matters, Gelb, a former high State Department official in the Carter administration, says that he is skeptical that progress toward a Middle East peace can be achieved in the next year or two.
news.title: U.S. Public Is Unconvinced on Need to Wage War Against Iraq, Says Council on Foreign Relations President Les Gelb

news.abstract: Afghanistan has achieved degree of stability in year since Hamid Karzai began governing, even if it is not yet united country with functioning multiethnic army; Karzai acknowledges some failures of his government, namely security and disarmament, and vows to tackle those issues more energetically in year ahead; Burhanuddin Rabbani, former president who last year opposed Karzai's presidency, now voices unreserved support for him and central government; American forces based in country now contemplate moving from combat operations toward development activities, deploying larger teams of civil affairs officers in 8 to 10 provincial centers to give boost to economic development; American officials say battle against Taliban and Al Qaeda is drawing to end and effort to win peace and help government establish its control countrywide is new target; economic condition of country remain precarious; regional warlords continue to flex enormous power, but Karzai is intent on winning them over by persuasion rather than force of arms (M)
news.title: Afghans Mark Year of Slowly Growing Stability

news.abstract: Interview with Adm James M Loy, undersecretary of transportation for security and head of Transportation Security Administration, which is scrambling to meet Dec 31 deadline for start of airport screening of all checked baggage; his can-do philosophy and lighthearted demeanor have won him praise from both parties on Capitol Hill and even within ranks of airlines and airport managers whose business he is restructuring; photo (M)
news.title: Safety Chief Tries to Make Travel Easy, Too

news.abstract: Operacion Triunfo, extremely popular Spanish reality television show that manufactures pop stars, prompts quixotic campaign by more than 100 musicians and critics, who complain about show's near monopoly of television music; show's contestants dominate Spanish record charts, and critics say show is elbowing out other music programs from prime-time space on public television (M)
news.title: Spain Loves a Pop Music Show, but Critics Hate the Reality

news.abstract: China releases Xu Wenli, its most prominent pro-democracy prisoners, sending him to exile and medical treatment in US; Wenli, who spent more than 16 of last 21 years in prison for his irrepressible advocacy of civil liberties, suffers from chronic and progressive infection with hepatitis B; his release signals China's strong desire for good relations with US; photo of Xu being greeted by his daughter at O'Hare Airport in Chicago (M)
news.title: BEIJING RELEASES LEADING DISSIDENT

news.abstract: Poland appeared set to award a contract to the Lockheed Martin Corporation to build 48 advanced fighter planes for the Polish Air Force at a cost of $3.5 billion.
news.title: Poland Said to Pick Lockheed for $3.5 Billion Fighter Deal

news.abstract: Reporter's Notebook on Gen Richard B Myers's visit to US air base in Kuwait; AH-64 Apache gunship, Army's main attack helicopter, and Air Force's RQ-1 Predator, propeller-driven robot plane that looks like upside-down spoon, could form deadly new tandem in US-led war in Iraq; Myers visit focuses on morale of US forces in region (S)
news.title: U.S. Army Finds Allies In the U.S. Air Force

news.abstract: Fertility rates in many European countries have plummeted over last decades, shifting one-child families close to statistical norm; World Health Orgn figures show Europe to be continent with lowest fertility rate; no West European country has total fertility rate of 2.1--marker that demographers say means exact replenishment of population; in United States rate is 2.0, which demographers attribute to greater immigration; trend in Europe has been evident for many years, but its slow-building consequences are now coming into starker relief; more West European countries are taking new steps to address specter of sharply winnowed and less competitive work forces, surfeits of retirees and pension systems that will need to be cut back deeply; fertility rates are starkest in East European countries, but trend hit Western Europe earlier, and has had more time to produce hand-wringing and soul-searching; among reasons for trend are that people are studying longer and marrying later, that contraception and abortion are readily available, that divorce is more common and that would-be parents' attachments to leisure time, conveniences and indulgences do not easily accommodate multiple children--or sometimes, any children at all; photo; graphs (L)
news.title: Persistent Drop in Fertility Reshapes Europe's Future

news.abstract: Pope John Paul II's Christmas message from St Peter's Square speaks out against prospect of war in Middle East and urges people not to succumb to fear of terrorism (M)
news.title: Pope Calls for War Fires to Be Extinguished

news.abstract: Energy Department predicts that Western dependence on Mideast oil will increase in two decades, even as Pres Bush seeks to reduce US reliance on such imports; forecast is that by 2025, 51 percent of world oil production will come from OPEC, which now produces 38 percent of world's oil; about two-thirds of OPEC production comes from Persian Gulf; graph (S)
news.title: Growing U.S. Need for Oil From the Mideast Is Forecast

news.abstract: State Department reports obtaining evidence that mass rapes of hundreds of girls and women were carried out by Burmese army in Shan Province, Myanmar, where military government has tried for years to suppress ethnic rebellion; says United States has expressed 'deep concern' about rapes and other abuses to Myanmar and urged government to punish guilty; US has also called on United Nations to probe charges, first made by human rights groups (M)
news.title: U.S. Says Evidence Confirms Reports of Mass Rapes by Burmese

news.abstract: In another major sign of preparations for a possible war against Iraq, the Navy has activated one of its two 1,000-bed hospital ships, the Comfort, to be sent for possible duty in the Persian Gulf.    Activating the Comfort signals that the Bush administration is preparing for large numbers of American casualties, and is ready to take the risk to back up its threat to use military force to disarm Iraq. The Comfort has 12 operating rooms and is equipped to deal with major trauma cases and casualties from chemical and biological weapons.
news.title: Navy Hospital Ship Is Activated for Duty

news.abstract: Foreign Min Joschka Fischer declines to rule out possibility of Germany voting for military action against Iraq in United Nations Security Council; comments reflect degree of flexibility absent in Chancellor Gerhard Schroder's earlier insistence that Germany would not support war even in event of affirmative vote in Security Council (S)
news.title: German Minister Softens Stance Against Iraq War

news.abstract: Iraq hands over to United Nations office in Baghdad list of more than 500 experts in development of ballistice missiles and nuclear, chemical or biological weapons, fulfilling one requirement of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1411; extent to which scientists will prove helpful in ferreting out any new information about Iraq's possible weapons of mass destruction remain open question; Kadhim Mijbel, second Iraqi scientists questioned by nuclear inspectors, suggests at news conference that all Iraqi scientists should demand that witness from government be present at interviews with inspectors and that no one should leave country to be interviewed (M)
news.title: Iraq Gives the U.N. a List Of 500 Weapons Experts

news.abstract: Many younger South Koreans are siding with North Korea in its confrontation with United States over its nuclear program and see their country as caught in middle of conflict; about 70 prostesters hold rally in Seoul against North Korea's nuclear program, but several thousands largely young people hold candlelight vigil outside US Embassy, demanding more equal partnership between Seoul and Washington and expulsion of 37,000 American troops stationed in South Korea; photo (M)
news.title: South Koreans Divided on North Korean Atom Threat

news.abstract: Ethnic Albanians in Kosovo are growing increasingly impatient with being Serbian province; they and Serbs would both opt for partition -- trading northern parts of Kosovo where most Serbs live for land inhabited by Albanians in other parts of southern Serbia -- even though it could open Pandora's box of border disputes, potentially threatening territorial integrity of both Bosnia and Macedonia; international bureaucrats who administer province want to defer decision on its ultimate status, but they are also eager to end their involvement there; map; photo; chronology of conflict in Kosovo (M)
news.title: A Restive Kosovo, Officially Still Serbian, Squirms Under the Status Quo

news.abstract: Senior US officials say Saudi Arabia has given them assurances that kingdom will make its airspace, air bases and important operations center at Prince Sultan Air Base outside Riyadh available to US in event of war with Iraq; are confident that Saudis will ultimately allow attack missions, which are more politically sensitive, to be flown from their soil; Saudis remain publicly noncommittal; uncertainty about Saudi cooperation led Pentagon to build alternative air command post in Qatar, where overall American command for Iraqi operations will be headquartered (M)
news.title: Saudis Are Said To Assure U.S. On Use of Bases

news.abstract: Australian government starts advertising campaign urging people to be alert to terrorist dangers at home; campaign takes pains not to single out Australia's Muslim population, which numbers about 400,000, and to emphasize country's diversity (M)
news.title: 'Let's Look Out for Australia,' An Antiterror Campaign Urges

news.abstract: Hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans fill streets of Caracas to declare their commitment to national strike, now in its 28th day, to force ouster of Pres Hugo Chavez; strike, joined by 30,000 oil workers, threatens to wreak havoc on nation, world's fifth-largest oil producer; photo (M)
news.title: Venezuela Strikers Keep Pressure on Chávez and Oil Exports

news.abstract: As the unofficial death toll for last week's attack in Grozny rose, President Vladimir V. Putin warned that militants are employing more violent tactics.
news.title: Death Toll Rises in Bombing of Russian Offices in Chechnya

news.abstract: Kenyans elect opposition leader Mwai Kibaki as their new president, in resounding defeat for party that has ruled over country for nearly four decades; result leaves no doubt about voters' opinion of 24-year rule of retiring president Daniel arap Moi, whose chosen successor Uhuru Kenyatta is rejected throughout country; this is first election governing party has lost since independence in 1963; election officials declare Kibaki winner as ballots are still being tabulated; say margin is so great that none of his four rivals stand chance; independent election watchers give Kibaki 63 percent of vote, compared with 20 percent for Kenyatta, second-place finisher; Kibaki is former finance minister and vice president to Moi who broke with him decade ago; has vowed to change Kenya's fortunes by turning tide on corruption, poverty and authoritarian rule; Moi's decision to retire, as required by country's Constitution, and to allow bitter rival to replace him is seen as milestone in development of Kenya's democracy; photos; map; brief recap of country's history since 1963 (L)
news.title: Kenya's Ruling Party Is Defeated After 39 Years

news.abstract: Bush administration's plan to use trade sanctions to force North Korea to abandon its nuclear bomb program worries South Korean investors who do business in North Korea; South Korea is North's second-largest trading partner after China; photo; map (L)
news.title: U.S. Plan for Trade Penalties for North Korea Worries South Korean Investors

news.abstract: Israeli Supreme Court rules that reserve soldiers cannot refuse to serve in occupied territories; ruling is setback to group of soldiers and officers who say they will serve elsewhere, but refuse to serve in West Bank or Gaza; group has 512 members but has not gained much political traction for its claim that occupation is corrupting Israeli society; group founder Lt David Zonshein is returned to military prison to serve remainder of sentence for refusing call-up; in latest violence, Israeli soldiers kill eight Palestinians in various incidents; photo (M)
news.title: Israel Rules Reserves Must Serve in Occupied Territories

news.abstract: Philippine police are no longer allowed to fire their weapons in celebration of New Year's Eve in effort to reduce accidental shootings; guns will be monitored with taped muzzles and hotline established for public to report illegal police firings; there are no laws preventing general population from celebrating with gunfire (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: Philippines: Police Can't Shoot For Fun

news.abstract: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Dublin pledges cooperation with any police investigation into sex abuse allegations against priests and says officers will have full access to church files; assurance comes after Cardinal Desmond Connell meets with abuse victims Ken Reilly and Marie Collins, who had demanded his resignation and threatened to stage protest (M)
news.title: Irish Church to Cooperate With Abuse Inquiry

news.abstract: Yemeni officials report three Americans killed at Baptist missionary hospital in central Yemen by man apparently belonging to small cell that plans to victimize both Westerners and secular Yemenis; fourth American is seriously wounded in attack; assailant, identified as Abed Abdul-Razak al-Kamil, sneaks semiautomatic rifle into hospital under his coat; Kamil surrenders to authorities and is arrested; this is latest in series of Islamic militant attacks against easily accessible American targets in region; officials in Washington say it is too early to know whether Kamil acted alone or is linked with Al Qaeda, whose leader Osama bin Laden has family origins in Yemen; guns are so common in Yemen that missionary hospital where attack occurred, in Jibla, has desk where visitors are supposed to check them; assailant easily evades site and bursts into room where staff meeting was taking place; those killed are hospital director William E Koehn, Dr Martha C Kyers and purchasing agent Kathleen A Gariety; pharmacist Donald W Caswell is shot but not killed; Kamil tells investigators he listened to speeches of Ali Mohammed Jarallah, member of Islamic Reform Party, who is being questioned by Yemeni authorities in connection with recent assassination of Socialist Party's deputy leader; Islamic militants are said to be resentful that missionary workers preach Christianity; photos; map (L)
news.title: 3 U.S. Citizens Slain in Yemen In Rifle Attack

news.abstract: China launches fourth unmanned spacecraft in program aimed toward eventual exploration of moon and Mars; Shenzhou IV lifts off from Gobi Desert on seven-day mission (S)
news.title: World Briefing | Asia: China: Another Step Toward Mars?
